summary: Jack Morris introduces "scaling compute on context" as the pursuit of depth in AI models against a fixed private corpus. He opens with Terence Tao's observation that AI has broad knowledge of public topics but lacks the deep, subconscious intuition a graduate student develops through years of focused study. Three scaling axes—more data, more compute, bigger models—powered the deep learning revolution, but these only operate on public data. Even post-training data from expert annotation companies is public by definition. Against your own corpus, the data axis is fixed, training from scratch is infeasible, and model size is predetermined, leaving compute as the sole scalable axis. The idealized problem: given a pre-trained model and an unstructured corpus D, produce a better model that knows D. Naive next-token prediction fails—training on 10K financial reports drives loss to 0.0001 but generation collapses, since the model memorizes without generalizing. Morris then surveys alternative approaches. KV compaction compresses data into KVs but only works for what already fits in context and skips gradients. On-policy distillation trains the model to think data is in context, but raises the question of what to distill—raw documents won't work, which is the gap the self-study technique in the cartridges paper addresses by generating Q&A pairs conditioned on D. Simulated pretraining via synthetic data conditioned on D is promising but overwrites some pretraining and requires a base model rather than the post-trained model most people start from. Unsupervised RL environments are similar but use RL loss instead of distillation. Every approach shares a ceiling: you define a dataset, train, and eventually the model absorbs everything, hitting a synthetic data wall with none of pretraining's scaling behavior. The property Morris wants is what made AlphaGo work—self-improvement where getting better makes training questions harder, so adding compute keeps buying depth instead of flattening out. Engram is pursuing techniques that make training gradually harder over time, producing a curve that keeps improving rather than plateauing.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Engram launch
sections.summary: Jack Morris introduces himself and Engram (Ngram), which launched the prior week. The talk frames the high-level problem of scaling compute on context rather than presenting detailed experiments.

sections.title: Terence Tao on breadth against depth
sections.summary: Morris cites Terence Tao's observation that AI knows every public mathematical topic and bridges literature gaps no human could, but lacks the deep, almost subconscious intuition a graduate student develops over years of focused study. Morris frames scaling compute on context as the pursuit of depth in AI.

sections.title: What models cannot know after training
sections.summary: Three examples: models do not know events after their training cutoff; they are bad at long-tail skills like AMD kernels due to sparse public data; and they know nothing about your personal or corporate life because all training data is public. Morris calls this the core problem of the current AI paradigm.

sections.title: Many names for the problem
sections.summary: The problem has many names—sleep time compute, continual learning, neural memory, write time compute, amortized inference—because the paradigm is early and unsolidified compared to pre-training or post-training.

sections.title: Three axes of scaling
sections.summary: The deep learning revolution rests on three axes: more data, more compute, bigger models. These produce compelling results but only on public data. Even post-training data from expert annotation companies is public by definition since it must be expressible to users.

sections.title: Why compute is the only axis left
sections.summary: For your own corpus, the data axis is fixed and training from scratch is infeasible because you need pre-trained world knowledge. This leaves compute as the only scalable axis. Morris notes the data budget is less fixed in practice but the idealized problem assumes a fixed corpus.

sections.title: Stating the problem properly
sections.summary: Given a pre-trained model and an unstructured corpus D, produce a new model theta* that knows D. The definition of 'know' is load-bearing and gives researchers leeway to propose different approaches.

sections.title: Just train on it, and why that fails
sections.summary: Naive next-token prediction on your data fails. Training on 10K financial reports drives loss to 0.0001 and the model knows the data perfectly, but generation collapses. The approach cannot generalize—no interesting properties emerge unless the question and answer are perfectly encoded in the data.

sections.title: Making the model think the data is in context: KV compaction
sections.summary: Morris explores tricking the model into thinking data is in context. KV compaction compresses D into a set of KVs, similar to how Claude Code or Codex does compaction. It works only for data small enough to fit in context, and it misses the magic of taking gradients on the data.

sections.title: On-policy distillation and what to distill
sections.summary: On-policy distillation trains the model to think text is in context, updating the model throughout training. It works but raises the question of what data to distill—raw documents won't do. The self-study technique from the cartridges paper generates Q&A pairs conditioned on D and trains the model to behave as if seeing D in context. Morris finds this close to desired behavior but with some unappealing properties.

sections.title: Simulating pretraining with synthetic data
sections.summary: Pretraining is amazing for knowledge acquisition. One approach is to craft synthetic data conditioned on D and continue pretraining. Morris finds this promising but notes caveats: it overwrites some pretraining, is difficult to scale, and requires a base model rather than the post-trained model most people actually start from.

sections.title: Unsupervised RL environments
sections.summary: Similar to the previous approach but using RL loss like GRPO instead of distillation. Morris finds all these approaches promising but missing a core component.

sections.title: The synthetic data wall
sections.summary: All proposed approaches share a ceiling: you define a dataset, train, and eventually the model learns all the data and saturates. This creates a synthetic data wall with none of pretraining's scaling behavior. Once you fit the data, you know something about D but cannot keep adding compute to gain more depth.

sections.title: Self-improvement and what AlphaGo had
sections.summary: The desired property is self-improvement, as in AlphaGo, where getting better makes training questions harder. The model generates data, gets better, then generates better data recursively. Early Engram experiments produced plateau curves, but more sophisticated techniques that make training gradually harder can produce a curve that keeps improving—building an increasingly better internal model of a user from their emails.
